headline.title: Pope Leo XIV plants a flag while AI's commerce and labor stack accelerates.

Illinois becomes the first US state to require third-party AI safety audits.

stories.title: Pope Leo XIV's Magnifica Humanitas plants a Catholic flag in the AI debate.
stories.toc_summary: Pope Leo XIV's first encyclical is dedicated entirely to AI. The text rejects equating machine intelligence with human personhood, warns of a 'new colonialism' built on health and behavioral data, and re-asserts that markets must remain subordinate to human dignity.
stories.quick_take: Pope Leo XIV — the first American pope and an Apple Watch wearer — has dedicated his first encyclical, *Magnifica Humanitas*, to AI [1][2]. Modeled on Leo XIII's 1891 *Rerum Novarum*, the document is neither doomer nor accelerationist; Catholic readers describe him as an 'AI realist' [1]. The strongest economic line — 'the pursuit of greater profits cannot justify choices that systematically sacrifice jobs' — frames markets as servants of human dignity, not the other way around [1]. A widely-cited paragraph 178 warns about a new digital colonialism built on population-level health and behavioral data [1]. Paragraph 99 explicitly denies machine personhood: AI 'does not undergo experiences, does not possess a body, does not feel joy or pain' and is doing 'statistical adaptation' rather than 'inner growth' [1]. A side note from KI Bubble: a LessWrong analysis using the Pangram detector flagged parts of the encyclical as 40-100% AI-generated, with the Vatican declining to comment so far [2].

bullets.label: First encyclical, first big move:
bullets.text: Encyclicals are not new doctrine — they reinterpret Catholic social teaching against new conditions; Leo XIV took the name as tribute to Leo XIII's industrial-revolution encyclical and put AI front and center [1].

bullets.label: Categorical separation:
bullets.text: Paragraph 99 says these systems 'merely imitate certain functions of human intelligence,' have no body, no moral conscience, no inner growth — pre-empting future debates about machine personhood [1].

bullets.label: Labor and dignity:
bullets.text: Leo's economic message — that profit cannot justify systematic job destruction — re-anchors Catholic social teaching for the AI labor disruption now underway [1].

bullets.label: Data as power:
bullets.text: The pope warns those who control health and behavioral data 'possess structural leverage over the future' and urges that shared knowledge become a true common good [1].

bullets.label: Authorship twist:
bullets.text: A LessWrong/Pangram analysis says portions of the text scored 40-100% AI-generated; if confirmed, the document arguing against AI displacing the human person was itself partly drafted by AI [2].

callout.label: BIG PICTURE
callout.text: One of the world's largest institutions has now formally declared AI a first-order moral question. Expect *Magnifica Humanitas* to be cited heavily in labor, hiring-bias and global-data-governance debates over the coming years [1].

sources.title: The AI Daily Brief — What the Pope Actually Said About AI

stories.title: Anthropic's Mythos has already surfaced 10,000+ severe vulnerabilities.
stories.toc_summary: Project Glasswing partners using Anthropic's still-private Mythos model have collectively identified over 10,000 high or critical software vulnerabilities. The bottleneck has shifted from finding bugs to patching them, and global regulators are demanding access.
stories.quick_take: Anthropic's late-week update on Project Glasswing — the limited rollout of its next-generation Mythos model to about 50 cybersecurity partners — claims more than 10,000 high- or critical-severity vulnerabilities found in just over a month, with less than a 10% false-positive rate on open-source repos [1]. Mozilla alone reported 271 fixes, more than 10x what it found with Opus 4.6; Palo Alto Networks shipped 5x as many patches [1]. The bottleneck has now flipped: maintainers are 'severely capacity constrained' and have asked Anthropic to slow disclosures so they can write fixes [1]. The exclusivity has triggered policy pushback: European, UK, Canadian, Australian and Asian governments are formally requesting access, and the White House chief of staff has approved use of Anthropic models at the NSA despite a prior Pentagon supply-chain risk designation [1].

bullets.label: The 10,000-bug claim:
bullets.text: Glasswing partners using Mythos have flagged 10,000+ high or critical CVEs in a little over a month, with sub-10% false positive rates on open-source code [1].

bullets.label: Real-world payoff:
bullets.text: One finance partner used Mythos to detect and block a $1.5M wire transfer to a threat actor who had compromised a customer account [1].

bullets.label: Jevons paradox for security engineers:
bullets.text: Box CEO Aaron Levy frames the result as a coming 'security engineer boom' — AI finds more bugs than humans can triage, escalating, not eliminating, demand for engineering judgment [1].

bullets.label: Government scramble:
bullets.text: EU, UK, Canada, Asia-Pacific governments all want Mythos; the Pentagon's Anthropic supply-chain block is being walked back, and NSA access is reportedly close [1].

bullets.label: Public-release timing:
bullets.text: Anthropic says no one — including itself — has safeguards strong enough yet to release a Mythos-class model publicly; a 'Claude Mythos 1 Preview' for trusted partners has been spotted in testing catalogs [1].

callout.label: WHY IT MATTERS
callout.text: Cybersecurity is the first commercial domain where a frontier-class AI is producing verifiable, large-scale economic output — and where the binding constraint instantly shifted from 'find bugs' to 'apply patches.' Expect every other AI-disruption debate to follow this shape [1].

sources.title: The AI Daily Brief — Project Glasswing / Mythos update

stories.title: White House approves a secret $9B classified inference cluster for the CIA and NSA.
stories.toc_summary: The New York Times reports that the White House signed off on a $9B budget request from the CIA and NSA to build their own Blackwell-based inference cluster, after admitting they can't run current frontier models on their classified systems.
stories.quick_take: According to the New York Times, the White House has approved a secret $9 billion budget request for the CIA and NSA to build their own AI inference cluster, after acknowledging the spy agencies cannot run frontier models on their existing classified systems [1]. The bulk of the spend goes to Nvidia Blackwell chips plus supporting infrastructure, against an industry-wide Blackwell shortage [1]. The White House issued a sharply-worded statement attacking the leak — but did not deny the substance [1]. Anthropic and the NSA are reportedly finalizing a contract that would let the agency run anthropic models in classified settings, ending a multi-month standoff in which the Pentagon had designated Anthropic a supply-chain risk over its usage restrictions [1].

bullets.label: Hardware push:
bullets.text: $9B targets a Blackwell-based inference cluster for both CIA and NSA — a backlog-driven race, not a one-off procurement [1].

bullets.label: Pentagon vs. spy agencies:
bullets.text: The Pentagon objected to Anthropic's no-autonomous-weapons / no-domestic-surveillance limits; intelligence agencies, already legally barred from domestic spying, are reportedly fine with the same limits [1].

bullets.label: OpenAI next:
bullets.text: Officials hope finalizing the Anthropic-NSA contract paves the way for an OpenAI deal that also covers spy agencies, after OpenAI's March Pentagon agreement explicitly excluded the NSA [1].

bullets.label: Strategic framing:
bullets.text: The NYT casts the move as the US intelligence community catching up after years of underfunding AI relative to the Pentagon and private labs [1].

callout.label: WHAT TO WATCH
callout.text: Whether the Anthropic-NSA contract closes in the next quarter, and whether OpenAI follows suit. Either deal makes 'frontier model + classified infrastructure' the new default for the US intelligence stack [1].

sources.title: The AI Daily Brief headlines / NYT reporting

stories.title: Deepseek makes its 75% discount permanent and closes in on a $10B raise.
stories.toc_summary: Deepseek V4's April promotional 75% discount is now its standing price, undercutting Opus 4.6 by 17x and GPT-5.4 by 4x. The company has told investors a $10B round at a $45B valuation is closing, with Chinese government and corporate participation.
stories.quick_take: Deepseek's V4 model launched in April with a temporary 75% discount on tokens; that price is now permanent, leaving the model at roughly 1/17th the cost of Opus 4.6 and 1/4 of GPT-5.4 at the time of those models' launches [1]. With Anthropic and OpenAI both having raised prices since, the gap has widened further [1]. In parallel, Deepseek management has told investors it is going ahead with its first-ever outside-funding round — about $10 billion, valuing the company at $45 billion, with the Chinese government's AI industry investment fund, Tencent and JD.com expected to participate [1]. Founder Liang Wenfang says the firm will keep open-sourcing models and chasing AGI rather than pivot to monetization [1].

bullets.label: Final price:
bullets.text: Deepseek V4 — roughly Opus 4.5-class — now lists at 44 cents per million input tokens and 87 cents per million output, against an Opus 4.6 that costs ~17x more [1].

bullets.label: Record raise:
bullets.text: If the $10B round closes at the reported $45B valuation, it would be the largest Chinese venture round to date [1].

bullets.label: Strategic message:
bullets.text: Bloomberg analysts cited in the brief frame this as Asia's AI models 'decoupling from the US' into a token-based industrial economy fueled by cheap power and one-person firms [1].

callout.label: LONG ARC
callout.text: US labs are betting on premium, frontier-only positioning; Chinese labs are betting on industrial-scale token pricing plus open weights. The latter is the cheaper option for a startup that just needs Opus-4.5-class reasoning today [1].

sources.title: The AI Daily Brief — Deepseek pricing & funding round

stories.title: xAI's Grok V9 medium finishes a 1.5T-parameter training run.
stories.toc_summary: Elon Musk announced that Grok V9 medium, a 1.5 trillion-parameter foundation model with substantial added Cursor coding data, has finished training. Fine-tuning is underway and reinforcement learning starts in days, with public release in 2-3 weeks.
stories.quick_take: Grok V9 medium — xAI's next foundation model — has finished its pre-training run at roughly 1.5 trillion parameters, Elon Musk announced [1]. He said evals 'look good,' a lot of Cursor coding data was added in supplementary training, fine-tuning is underway, reinforcement learning begins in a few days, and the model should be in public release in 2-3 weeks [1]. The model is meant as a 'major improvement' over the 0.5T V8 small currently serving all Grok production traffic, especially on hard coding tasks [1]. In parallel, xAI rolled out Grok Build — its Codex/Claude-Code competitor — to Super Grok and X Premium users; one developer who tried it called it 'surprisingly good, much better than I expected. The harness is solid, models are very fast, and it already seems less buggy than Claude' [1].

bullets.label: Scale and code-mix:
bullets.text: 1.5T-parameter base model, with deliberate emphasis on Cursor-derived coding data — xAI is going hard at the coding assistant market [1].

bullets.label: Release cadence:
bullets.text: Fine-tuning → RL → public release inside ~3 weeks would put V9 in users' hands before the end of June [1].

bullets.label: Grok Build broadens out:
bullets.text: Previously only on the $300/mo Grok Heavy tier, the coding harness is now available to Super Grok and X Premium subscribers [1].

callout.label: WHAT TO WATCH
callout.text: Whether Grok V9 medium's real-world coding performance matches its training data implication — and whether xAI's positioning as 'SpaceX AI' (rather than a standalone lab) starts producing visible strategic moves [1].

sources.title: The AI Daily Brief — Grok V9 training

stories.title: Anthropic's Mythos cracks Erdős Problem #90 with a simpler proof than OpenAI's.
stories.toc_summary: Anthropic technical staffer Sholto Douglas says Mythos has solved the same long-standing Erdős conjecture OpenAI claimed earlier — and reached the same result with a simpler proof.
stories.quick_take: Sholto Douglas, a member of Anthropic's technical staff, posted that the company's still-private Mythos model has also solved Erdős Problem #90, reaching the same result that OpenAI announced earlier — but with a simpler proof [1]. The claim, currently a one-sentence X post passed through The Rundown, adds to a small but growing list of decades-old open math problems that recent frontier models have nudged forward [1].

bullets.label: Same conclusion, cleaner proof:
bullets.text: If verified, Mythos's proof would be a non-trivial improvement on OpenAI's already-celebrated solution [1].

bullets.label: Frontier math is now a measurable benchmark:
bullets.text: Solving Erdős-style conjectures has become a status marker between labs much like Olympiad scores were last year [1].

callout.label: WHY IT MATTERS
callout.text: Independent verification matters here: the labs have an incentive to overstate. But if 'simpler proof' holds up, Mythos's reasoning style — not just its size — is the news [1].

sources.title: The Rundown AI — Sholto Douglas on X

stories.title: Anthropic publishes its Claude containment and blast-radius strategy.
stories.toc_summary: Anthropic's engineering blog details how it now grants Claude access powerful enough to destroy internal services — and how aggressive sandboxing keeps that access safe. The post applies across claude.ai, Claude Code and Cowork.
stories.quick_take: Anthropic published its engineering team's containment strategy for Claude, applicable across claude.ai, Claude Code and Cowork [1]. The headline: twelve months ago, Anthropic would have refused access patterns that today are routine — including access powerful enough to take down internal Anthropic services [1]. The shift is not weaker security; it is sandboxing. Rather than blanket-blocking risky permissions, the team now wraps potentially destructive actions in tight 'blast-radius' cages, freeing the model's capabilities to grow inside those cages [1]. The result, Anthropic claims, is materially higher developer productivity inside the company [1].

bullets.label: From deny-by-default to sandbox-by-default:
bullets.text: Permissions that were untouchable a year ago — like writes that can knock out an internal service — are now routine, behind tight isolation [1].

bullets.label: Blast-radius engineering as a discipline:
bullets.text: Anthropic argues every action an agentic worker takes is a potential production event; engineering teams need to formalize the radius of damage of each call [1].

bullets.label: Cross-product applicability:
bullets.text: The same containment strategy underpins claude.ai, Claude Code and Cowork — i.e., this is Anthropic's house style, not a one-product policy [1].

callout.label: DO THIS TODAY
callout.text: If you ship anything where an AI agent can act in your stack — read the post, then re-audit your own permissions model around 'what is the maximum damage one bad call can do, and how do I cap it?' [1]

sources.title: Anthropic engineering blog — How we contain Claude

stories.title: Google's I/O 2026 turns Search, Gemini, YouTube and Gmail into a single Universal Cart.
stories.toc_summary: Google's Universal Cart bundles purchases from Search, Gemini, YouTube and Gmail into one session. The agent watches prices after add-to-cart, warns on product incompatibility and checks card perks against the basket.
stories.quick_take: Google used I/O 2026 to unveil Universal Cart — a single cross-product cart that bundles purchases initiated in Search, Gemini, YouTube and Gmail into one checkout session [1][2]. The agent watches prices after items go into the cart, warns about product incompatibility, and checks credit-card perks against basket contents [1]. The Everlast briefing frames it bluntly: this is not a new marketplace, it's a buy-now layer that spans the entire Google ecosystem [1]. If it scales, the classic 'open a shop tab in a browser' workflow is structurally obsolete [1][2].

bullets.label: One cart, four surfaces:
bullets.text: Search, Gemini, YouTube and Gmail are now the same store from the user's perspective [1][2].

bullets.label: Active, not passive:
bullets.text: Post-add price watching, compatibility warnings and card-perk checks turn the cart into an agent, not a list [1].

bullets.label: Strategic frame:
bullets.text: Buy-now functionality across Google products, not a competitor marketplace — Google's defensive AND offensive play against Amazon and Shopify-native checkout [2].

callout.label: BIG PICTURE
callout.text: The browser tab as 'shop frontend' is going the way of the address book. Agentic commerce wants to collapse search-discover-decide-buy into one conversation — and Google is the first hyperscaler to actually ship it across all its surfaces [1][2].

sources.title: Everlast AI (WhatsApp) — Google Universal Cart
KI Bubble — Google I/O 2026 Universal Cart write-up

stories.title: Gmail's AI Inbox gets draft replies, a to-do hub and inline doc links.
stories.toc_summary: Gmail's AI Inbox now produces personalized draft replies, runs a task panel on the home screen, and surfaces matching Google Doc/Sheet/Slide links next to each task. The inbox shifts from passive triage to active workbench.
stories.quick_take: Google rolled out three concrete upgrades to Gmail's AI Inbox at I/O [1][2]. First, the inbox now generates personalized draft replies you only need to confirm and send [1]. Second, the to-do list runs through its own home-screen panel — tick a task, dismiss a suggestion or mark a mail read in one click [1][2]. Third, when a task implies a document, Gmail surfaces the matching Google Doc, Sheet or Slide link right next to it [1][2]. Gmail flips from passive inbox to active workbench: the inbox is no longer just prioritizing, it is staging answers and tasks for you [2].

bullets.label: Draft-on-demand:
bullets.text: Per-thread, personalized drafts that you approve rather than write [1].

bullets.label: Native to-do panel:
bullets.text: Inbox-derived tasks now live in their own home-screen panel with single-click actions [1][2].

bullets.label: Doc surface:
bullets.text: If a task references a doc, the relevant Doc/Sheet/Slide is one tap away — no more re-searching Drive [2].

callout.label: DO THIS TODAY
callout.text: If you triage mail by hand, try one full work day where you let Gmail's draft-reply suggestion be your first draft and edit, not your blank page [1].

stories.title: Google DeepMind launches Gemini for Science aimed directly at researchers.
stories.toc_summary: Gemini for Science is a research-team-targeted bundle of DeepMind's frontier model — pitched at scientists rather than consumer chat users. DeepMind doubles down on the segment where it already holds AlphaFold's Nobel and AlphaGenome.
stories.quick_take: Google DeepMind launched Gemini for Science, a research-team-targeted bundle of its frontier model [1][2]. The pitch is to scientists who want to use Gemini directly for their work rather than click through a consumer chat interface [1]. The move cements DeepMind's positioning in the science segment — the same lab that won the 2024 Nobel with AlphaFold and that overhauled DNA annotation with AlphaGenome [1]. While OpenAI and Anthropic chase the enterprise market, DeepMind is doubling down on the domain where AI today most directly produces verifiable breakthroughs: research [1][2].

bullets.label: Researcher-first packaging:
bullets.text: Tools, agents and integrations targeted at the workflow of a lab, not the cadence of a Slack DM [1].

bullets.label: DeepMind moat:
bullets.text: AlphaFold, AlphaGenome and now a Gemini bundle that ties it together — the lab is converting its science wins into an enterprise-style science product [1][2].

callout.label: LONG ARC
callout.text: If 2024-25 was about AI assistants for white-collar work, 2026 is shaping up to be the year AI workbenches for actual scientific R&D become the highest-value AI product line [1][2].

sources.title: Everlast AI (WhatsApp) — Gemini for Science
KI Bubble — Gemini for Science

stories.title: Google Omni renders cinematic drone POV from a hand-drawn camera path.
stories.toc_summary: Google Omni converts a sketched camera trajectory into a photorealistic drone-POV clip. The breakthrough is control: filmmakers now plan shots like a storyboard and let the model render them.
stories.quick_take: Google Omni — Google's video generator — turns a hand-drawn camera trajectory into a photorealistic drone-POV clip [1][2]. Camera control has been the persistent weakness of video models: Pika, Runway and Veo could ship usable clips, but the camera path itself was largely accidental [1]. Explicit, sketchable camera paths flip that: filmmakers plan shots like a storyboard and render the move directly [1]. The implication for ad spots, architecture viz and feature-film pre-vis is concrete — workflows that previously required a real drone crew now collapse to one prompt-plus-sketch pair [1][2].

bullets.label: Control is the breakthrough:
bullets.text: Sketch the trajectory, the model renders the rest — the missing primitive for usable AI cinematography [1].

bullets.label: Cost collapse:
bullets.text: Drone crews, location permits and B-roll shoots are partially substitutable today for sketch-then-render [1][2].

bullets.label: Closes a gap vs. peers:
bullets.text: Pika, Runway and Veo have lacked deterministic camera control; Omni's sketch input is the simplest answer yet shipped [1].

callout.label: WHAT TO WATCH
callout.text: Whether Veo and Runway add an equivalent sketch-the-camera-path primitive in their next releases. Camera control is now table stakes [1].

sources.title: Everlast AI (WhatsApp) — Google Omni
KI Bubble — Google Omni drone POV

stories.title: DuckDuckGo installs jump 30% as users reject Google's AI-only search.
stories.toc_summary: Days after Google replaced its classic blue-link results page with AI-generated answers at I/O 2026, DuckDuckGo reports a 30% surge in app installs. Web publishers lose the click; aggregators capture the answer.
stories.quick_take: Google used I/O 2026 to remove its classic list of blue links and replace them with AI-generated answers — and within days, DuckDuckGo reports a 30% surge in app installs [1]. The structural read: the search engine becomes an answer engine, and the source page disappears behind the answer card [1]. For any publisher that lives on web traffic, that's a direct hit; for any business that doesn't build its own direct channels (newsletter, app, community), referral traffic is now mediated by an aggregator that monetizes the in-between step itself [1].

bullets.label: The trigger:
bullets.text: I/O 2026's AI-only results page (no blue links by default) produced an immediate user backlash large enough to move DuckDuckGo's app install curve [1].

bullets.label: 30% in days:
bullets.text: App-store install velocity rarely moves 30% on UX alone — this is a referendum [1].

bullets.label: Strategic implication:
bullets.text: If your distribution depends on Google referral traffic, the answer card is now the page; build direct channels yesterday [1].

callout.label: DO THIS TODAY
callout.text: Audit your traffic mix. If Google organic is more than half of it, the next quarterly review is where you need to defend (or accept) that exposure [1].

sources.title: TechCrunch — DuckDuckGo installs +30% as users reject Google AI search

stories.title: NVIDIA Vera CPU beats x86 by 1.5x on first Phoronix benchmarks.
stories.toc_summary: NVIDIA's Vera — an ARM CPU built specifically for agentic AI workloads — posts 1.5x overall performance, 2x faster Linux kernel compilation, and 4x STREAM-TRIAD memory bandwidth vs. leading x86 chips in the first Phoronix benchmarks.
stories.quick_take: NVIDIA's Vera CPU — an ARM design built specifically for agentic AI workloads — has shipped its first independent benchmark numbers via Phoronix [1]. Against the top x86 processors: 1.5x overall performance, 2x faster Linux kernel compilation, 4x STREAM-TRIAD memory bandwidth [1]. The point isn't 'ARM beats x86' — it's that NVIDIA is no longer positioning the CPU as GPU-adjacent furniture. The CPU now sits at the center of the AI factory's data flow, from memory controller to transformer block [1]. If you were tracking only NVIDIA's GPU roadmap, the AI-factory product line just became vertically integrated [1].

bullets.label: Workload focus:
bullets.text: Vera is purpose-built for agentic AI — memory bandwidth and IO matter more than raw single-thread numbers, hence the 4x STREAM-TRIAD gap [1].

bullets.label: Compile-time win:
bullets.text: 2x faster Linux kernel compilation is the developer-experience headline, especially for shops running large internal codebases [1].

bullets.label: Strategic frame:
bullets.text: NVIDIA's full stack is now: GPU + ARM CPU + DGX systems + Spectrum-X networking — Vera plugs the CPU hole in the vertical [1].

callout.label: WHAT TO WATCH
callout.text: When Vera becomes orderable as part of NVIDIA's DGX line, and how Intel and AMD price-position their next data-center CPUs against an integrated NVIDIA stack [1].

sources.title: NVIDIA Blog — Vera CPU Phoronix benchmarks

stories.title: Inference startups keep outgrowing the hyperscalers.
stories.toc_summary: Fireworks, Baseten and Together AI were supposed to die when AWS, Azure and GCP rolled their own open-model inference. Instead, demand for tuned inference is outrunning what the hyperscalers can ship.
stories.quick_take: A year ago the consensus thesis was that inference specialists like Fireworks, Baseten and Together AI would be eaten by the hyperscalers as AWS, Azure and GCP launched custom inference layers for open-source models [1]. The opposite happened: the specialists are growing fast despite a structurally awkward business model — renting NVIDIA capacity on AWS, Azure and GCP, layering optimized open-source stacks (Llama, Qwen, DeepSeek) on top, and reselling that as a service [1]. Gross margins are compressed but demand for custom inference is outpacing what the hyperscalers' own layers can absorb [1].

bullets.label: The thesis that failed:
bullets.text: Hyperscalers were supposed to commodify inference; instead, they couldn't keep up with custom workloads [1].

bullets.label: Stack picture:
bullets.text: Specialists rent GPU capacity from the same hyperscalers, then add Llama/Qwen/DeepSeek tuning — squeezed margins, growing volume [1].

bullets.label: Open-source tailwind:
bullets.text: Llama, Qwen and DeepSeek's release cadence keeps generating new optimization opportunities the specialists are faster to ship than AWS or Azure [1].

callout.label: BIG PICTURE
callout.text: Inference is moving the way CDN did: hyperscalers run the substrate, specialists run the tuned layer customers actually buy. Expect Fireworks/Baseten/Together to look more like Cloudflare than like AWS [1].

sources.title: The Information — Boom times for inference providers

stories.title: Figure ships humanoids into JCPenney's distribution center.
stories.toc_summary: Figure — valued at $39B — has signed a deal with Catalyst Brands (JCPenney, Aéropostale, Brooks Brothers) to put humanoids into the Reno distribution center's Joey Pouch sortation system. First production deployment after the 200-hour autonomy livestream.
stories.quick_take: Figure has signed a major deal with Catalyst Brands — the parent company of JCPenney, Aéropostale and Brooks Brothers — to deploy humanoid robots in the Reno, Nevada distribution center, handling the Joey Pouch sortation system [1][2]. Huang invoked wabi-sabi — the beauty of imperfection — to argue uniquely human qualities will become more prized across domains [1]. stories.title: Stanford finds clear racial bias in AI hiring tools across 4M applications.
stories.toc_summary: A Stanford study of 4 million applications across 156 employers found that AI hiring tools — particularly Pymetrics — produce 'clear racial disparities.' 10.62% of positions show adverse impact against Black applicants, 5.32% against Asians, with 42 models shared across employers compounding the problem.
stories.quick_take: A Stanford study of 4 million job applications across 156 employers found 'clear racial disparities' in AI hiring tools, with Black and Asian applicants disproportionately screened out and some facing rejection at every company [1]. Researchers analyzed Pymetrics' per-position data: 10.62% of positions show adverse impact against Black applicants, 5.32% against Asians [1]. The problem compounds: 42 models are shared across employers, so rejection at one can trigger rejection at another using the same model [1]. 4% of applicants who applied to 10 positions were rejected from all of them — higher than independent decision-making would predict [1]. Researchers caution that today's LLM-based hiring tools work differently from those studied (2018-2022), but the structural lesson holds: bias can creep in through shared infrastructure in unknown ways [1].

bullets.label: Pymetrics-specific evidence:
bullets.text: 10.62% adverse-impact rate for Black applicants, 5.32% for Asian — measured at the position level across 156 employers [1].

bullets.label: Shared-model compounding:
bullets.text: 42 models shared across employers means one bad screen can lock you out of an industry segment [1].

bullets.label: Reject-everywhere rate:
bullets.text: 4% of applicants to 10 positions got rejected at all of them — statistically inconsistent with independent decisions [1].

bullets.label: Caveat:
bullets.text: Today's LLM-driven hiring tools differ from the 2018-2022 systems studied — but the shared-infra failure mode generalizes [1].

callout.label: WHY IT MATTERS
callout.text: If even one major vendor in any sensitive AI domain has a bias, multiple downstream customers inherit it silently. The Illinois audit law (story 22) is the policy-side response — the Stanford paper is the empirical evidence the law needs [1].

sources.title: Algorithmic Hiring paper via The Rundown / FT

stories.title: Gulf states and Singapore lead global AI adoption — Germany is missing from the top 10.

stories.quick_take: Worldwide, just 17.8% of working-age adults use AI regularly — about one in six [1]. The leaders, though, are the Gulf states: UAE 70%, Singapore 63% — two states deliberately deploying AI as a national positioning strategy [1]. Europe follows closely: Norway 49%, Ireland and France 48%, Spain 44%, then UK and Netherlands at 42% [1]. The conspicuous absentee from the top 10: Germany [1]. The takeaway is direct — where governments and firms pull AI into daily work early, a measurable workforce edge develops; where they wait, they fall behind in a field that resorts annually [1].

bullets.text: UAE (70%) and Singapore (63%) treat AI adoption as industrial policy; the rankings reflect that bet [1].

stories.toc_summary: Between 2000 and 2023, U.S. job categories with no dominant software vendor grew the most: nail and foot care +413%, HR managers +376%, event planners +282%, massage therapists +276%, compliance +202%. The common thread: these are open ground for AI-native applications.
stories.quick_take: Between 2000 and 2023, the fastest-growing U.S. job categories share a trait: there is no dominant software vendor sitting on the market [1]. Nail and foot-care professionals grew 413%, HR managers 376%, event planners 282%, massage therapists 276%, compliance 202% [1]. The mainstream SaaS playbook has skipped these segments — they still run on Excel, phone calls and notebooks [1]. That's exactly what makes them the most interesting playing fields for AI-native applications: where Excel still rules, an agent can orchestrate bookings, run compliance, retain customers [1]. Entry barriers collapse the moment AI hits classical-software-grade trustworthiness [1].

bullets.label: Strategic implication:

stories.title: LinkedIn co-founder Guericke: three mistakes German founders keep making.
stories.toc_summary: LinkedIn co-founder Konstantin Guericke names the three patterns he sees breaking German AI startups: overestimating customer change-readiness, underestimating sales and marketing, taking too much VC too early. He also argues LLMs are far from exhausted.
stories.quick_take: LinkedIn co-founder Konstantin Guericke — a German Stanford alum who co-founded LinkedIn with Reid Hoffman in 2003 — sat down with Leonard Schmedding on a hike through Palo Alto and laid out three patterns that keep breaking German startups [1][2]. Mistake one: founders overestimate how quickly customers change habits — even a clearly better product spreads slowly [1]. Mistake two: sales and marketing are underrated; most German founders come from MBA or tech backgrounds and underestimate the work between product and market [1]. Mistake three: too much VC too early — early millions couple you to the VC return profile, which only fits OpenAI-scale bets, not consultancy or niche SaaS [1]. On LLMs specifically, Guericke uses Nvidia's polygon-vs-NURBS win as his analogy: LLMs are not a dead end, they're a dominant ecosystem that will keep being optimized; the interesting frontier is at the edges — multimodal sensors, smart glasses, smartphone-grade measurement [1].

bullets.label: Customer habit change is slow:
bullets.text: Founders are in the top percentile of switching willingness; their customers are not [1].

bullets.label: Sales and marketing are the bottleneck:
bullets.text: Most German founders are tech or MBA — both underestimate the work between product and market [1].

bullets.label: VC too early kills optionality:
bullets.text: Big rounds lock you to OpenAI-scale return profiles; few business models actually fit that [1].

bullets.label: LLMs are not exhausted:
bullets.text: Ecosystem-driven optimization curves outrun architectural alternatives. The interesting move is multimodal, not architectural [1].

bullets.label: Silicon Valley is not mandatory:
bullets.text: Guericke warns about survivorship bias — German founders should go for multicultural and hands-on exposure, not as a default visa play [1].

callout.label: DO THIS TODAY
callout.text: If you're a founder weighing your next round, run Guericke's three mistakes against your last 12 months and see which one you've already committed [1].

stories.title: Mechanosynthesis: researchers build carbon structures atom by atom.
stories.toc_summary: Forty years after Drexler's 'Engines of Creation', a research group is building carbon structures on hydrogenated silicon — atom by atom — using an inverted scanning tunneling microscope. Programmable manufacturing at the level of individual chemical bonds.
stories.quick_take: Eric Drexler's vision from *Engines of Creation* is leaving the realm of speculation [1]. A research group is now building carbon structures directly on hydrogenated silicon, atom by atom, controlled by an inverted scanning tunneling microscope [1]. The technique — *mechanosynthesis* — is programmable manufacturing at the scale of individual chemical bonds [1]. If it scales, the line between software and matter collapses: you stop writing code and start writing atoms [1]. Four decades after Drexler's manifesto, the first reliable step toward computronium, programmable matter and self-replicating machines is happening in a real lab [1].

bullets.label: First production-scale primitive:
bullets.text: Carbon-on-silicon, atom-by-atom, controlled by an inverted STM [1].

bullets.label: Strategic implication:
bullets.text: Software-to-matter convergence is no longer purely theoretical [1].

callout.label: LONG ARC
callout.text: Mechanosynthesis is the kind of background development that gets ignored for years and then defines a decade. Watch the throughput and error-rate numbers as the lab scales [1].

stories.title: University of Rochester solar device makes drinking water and lithium from seawater.
stories.toc_summary: A new solar-thermal device at the University of Rochester turns ocean water into fresh water and simultaneously extracts lithium — using sunlight as its only energy input. Two scarce resources from one input.
stories.quick_take: A new solar-thermal device from the University of Rochester turns ocean water into fresh water and simultaneously extracts lithium from the brine — with sunlight as the only energy input [1]. Two of the era's scarcest resources from one input: fresh water for the three billion people in water-stressed regions, lithium for every battery, EV and grid-storage facility of the next decades [1]. If it scales, the geopolitical lever shifts: water rights and Chinese lithium processing lose their choke-point function; the sun substitutes for the conflict, and the ocean becomes a feedstock for the next energy order [1].

bullets.label: Two outputs, one input:
bullets.text: Sun-powered solar-thermal device co-produces drinking water and lithium from seawater [1].

bullets.label: Geopolitical implication:
bullets.text: If commercialized, China's lithium processing dominance is partially defanged, and water-scarcity politics shift [1].

callout.label: WHAT TO WATCH
callout.text: Whether Rochester's team publishes throughput and cost numbers credible enough for a pilot. Lab demos in this category are common; commercial-grade economics are not [1].

stories.toc_summary: The Rundown's latest guide walks through turning a messy weekly marketing review into a repeatable Cowork workflow — folders, skills for input ingestion, drafting and publishing, plus a feedback loop that makes each week smarter than the last.
stories.quick_take: The Rundown's latest training guide walks through turning a messy weekly marketing review into a repeatable Claude Cowork workflow [1]. The recipe: a `marketing-metrics-review/` folder structure with `inputs/`, `working/`, `skills/` and `outputs/` [1]. A first skill summarizes Slack, checks Gmail for sales updates, reviews GA revenue and pulls Drive meeting notes into `inputs/` [1]. A second skill drafts the report, leadership brief, Slack update and action items from those inputs [1]. A third publishing skill automates delivery [1]. editorial.title: The day a pope, a warehouse and an audit law spoke the same language.
editorial.intro: Today's feed reads like a strangely coordinated chorus. Pope Leo XIV publishes the Catholic Church's first encyclical on AI. Figure deploys humanoids into a JCPenney warehouse. Illinois becomes the first US state to require third-party audits of AI labs' safety claims. Anthropic publishes its blast-radius engineering doctrine. Three institutions you'd never expect to brief in unison just made the same argument from different angles: AI is leaving the demo phase, and the rules around it now have to be load-bearing.
editorial.body: The encyclical sets the moral floor — humans are not optimization targets, the value of a person isn't a benchmark score, and data ownership is the next great power asymmetry. Illinois converts that moral floor into a statutory one: lab safety claims become independently verifiable, not marketing copy. Figure and Catalyst Brands take the same week to show what's at stake on the labor side, sliding humanoids into the kind of brutal sortation work that historically employed three shifts of humans. Anthropic's blast-radius post is the engineering complement: when models can take down internal services, sandboxing replaces blanket bans. Meanwhile, the commerce stack is reorganizing under our feet. Google's Universal Cart, the Gmail AI Inbox, Gemini for Science, Google Omni and the OpenRouter Series B all add up to the same thesis — AI is becoming the substrate, not a feature. And the price floor keeps dropping: Deepseek makes its 75% discount permanent, Xiaomi cuts MiMo by up to 99%, Anthropic and OpenAI raise prices in the other direction. The split between premium-frontier and industrial-token pricing is now structural, not promotional.
editorial.pull_quote: Three institutions you'd never expect to brief in unison just made the same argument from different angles: the rules around AI now have to be load-bearing.
editorial.outro: Read individually, today's items are scattered. Read together, they describe the same handoff: from a 'what can AI do?' decade to a 'what should we let AI do, and what proof do we require?' decade. The labs, the labor market, the regulators and now even the Vatican are all answering that question in their own dialects. The fact they're all answering it at once is the news.

takeaway.label: IF YOU TAKE ONE THING FROM THIS
takeaway.text: The interesting AI question in mid-2026 is no longer capability — it's institutional fit. Whoever builds the auditing, sandboxing, pricing and labor-transition infrastructure around capable models wins the next phase, regardless of who has the bigger model.
